idiom_name: DbProviderFactory-style abstract class with Create* methods (System.Data.Common)
implementation_notes: .NET ships the pattern for data access: System.Data.Common.DbProviderFactory is an abstract class with one Create* operation per product kind (DbConnection, DbCommand, DbParameter, DbDataAdapter), and DbProviderFactories resolves a factory instance from a provider invariant name at runtime. Write your own families in the same shape - an abstract class or interface per family - and let Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection own selection by registering the concrete factory (singleton or scoped) and injecting the abstraction; use Func<T> delegates only when a single product needs a test seam. Because concrete factories are stateless, registering them as singletons keeps one family for the whole object graph. For closed family sets, a sealed record of factory methods is more concise and gives compile-time exhaustiveness.
pitfalls: Registering a different concrete family for transient resolutions lets one workflow mix variants; bind exactly one selected family in the composition root and choose singleton or scoped lifetime according to its state and request boundary.
Created products such as DbConnection implement IDisposable: the client owns and must dispose them, not the factory.
Adding a product kind extends DbProviderFactory-like base classes for every provider: expect a breaking change across all implementations, so keep the interface minimal.

Calling DbProviderFactory.CreateDataSourceEnumerator() asks the selected provider for its own discovery object; an empty or unsupported enumeration says nothing about whether the provider can create connections or commands, so select the provider explicitly and handle provider-specific support.
Using Activator.CreateInstance to instantiate the factory defeats the DI container's lifetime management; resolve the factory from the container instead.
